opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the initial impact was pretty modest. When we started working on learning from demonstration, behavior cloning wasn't the hot topic it is today. A lot of people in the community saw it as a fairly naive approach. You just regress actions from observations, and everyone knew the textbook problems: compounding errors, distribution shift, the policy drifting into states it has never seen and then falling apart. So there was a fair amount of skepticism, and reinforcement learning was getting much more of the attention.

What we were trying to show was that if you're thoughtful about the structure, you can get surprisingly far. That means how you collect the data, how you represent the task, and how you break long-horizon tasks into pieces the model can actually learn. A lot of my early work was about hierarchy and compositionality. Robots shouldn't have to learn a ten-minute task as one monolithic mapping. They can reuse sub-skills and reason about what comes next.

At the time, I'd say the reception was "interesting, but does it scale?" And that was a fair question, because we didn't have the data or the model capacity to really answer it. Looking back, I think the more lasting contribution was less any single result and more helping to build the case that imitation learning, done carefully, is a serious path for robot learning. That includes the benchmarks and datasets that let people actually compare methods. Plenty of other groups pushed that idea forward too.

Now, with large-scale teleoperation data and foundation-model-style policies, behavior cloning is basically the backbone of a lot of the field. It's a bit funny to see. The core idea didn't change much. What changed was the data, the compute, and the community's willingness to invest in it. So I'd describe the early impact as planting seeds rather than an immediate splash, and I'm happy to see where they've grown.

r001.rationale: The response describes modest early impact as stemming from skepticism about behavior cloning and attention going to reinforcement learning. It does not mention COVID-19 shutdowns.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'd say the initial impact was less about any single result and more about shifting what people thought was worth trying.

When we started pushing on behavior cloning seriously, a lot of the field had kind of written it off. The conventional wisdom was that imitation learning suffers from compounding errors, that you'd always need reinforcement learning or some kind of online correction on top of it to get anything robust. And that's not wrong in theory. But what we found, especially through the work on large-scale human demonstration datasets and the robomimic study, was that a lot of the supposed failures of behavior cloning were really failures of the data and the design choices around it, not the paradigm itself. Things like how you collect demonstrations, how consistent the operators are, whether you use history, how you model multimodal actions. When you got those details right, plain supervised learning from demonstrations worked way better than people expected.

So I think the early impact was giving people permission to take the simple thing seriously again. It made a case that if you invest in good data and a careful learning setup, you can get surprisingly far without a reward function, without simulation, without any of the machinery people assumed was mandatory. And that lined up well with what was happening in the rest of machine learning, where scale and data were turning out to matter more than clever algorithms.

The part I'm a little more measured about is that it also made some people overcorrect. Behavior cloning is a great starting point, but it's still bounded by the demonstrator, and generalization to things you've never shown the robot is still the hard problem. So I'd say the initial impact was real and mostly positive, but it opened a door rather than solving anything. The interesting work is what's come after, figuring out how to go beyond the demonstrations rather than just reproducing them.

r001.rationale: The response describes the initial impact as renewing interest in behavior cloning; it does not attribute negligible impact to COVID-19 shutdowns.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the initial excitement from the practical impact. Behavior cloning offered a very intuitive way to teach a robot: show it what to do, then train it to imitate those demonstrations. That made it a useful starting point for learning skills that are difficult to program by hand.

But getting a robot to reproduce a demonstration is different from getting it to work reliably. Small mistakes can put it in situations that weren’t represented in the training data, and then those mistakes compound. So I’d assess the initial impact in terms of both the capabilities it enabled and the limitations it exposed. It gave us a foundation, while making the questions of generalization and recovery much more concrete.

r001.rationale: The response discusses behavior cloning’s usefulness and reliability limits but does not attribute negligible initial impact to COVID-19 shutdowns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the initial impact was showing that behavior cloning could be a practical way to teach robots useful skills. Instead of manually specifying every movement, you could collect demonstrations and train a policy to imitate them.

But it also made the limitations very clear. A robot can perform well on situations represented in the demonstrations and then struggle when something changes slightly. Small mistakes compound, and the robot ends up in states it hasn’t seen before. So I’d assess the impact as both an encouraging proof of concept and a starting point for asking how we make imitation learning more robust and generalizable.

r001.rationale: The response describes behavior cloning as an encouraging proof of concept, but does not attribute negligible initial impact to COVID-19 shutdowns.
